findings.text: Dump iteration state keeps a current position counter, a resume offset supplied by the caller, a destination message buffer, and a reference to the active dump callback. The position advances per domain visited and is compared against the resume offset to skip already reported entries.

Debug helper pairs a performance domain pointer with a numeric state index. It is allocated per domain with one element per state and passed as private context to per state attribute readers so each file can locate its domain and row.

Lookup by numeric identifier scans the global domain list and returns the matching domain or a null indicator when absent. The full implementation serializes the scan with the list mutex; a header fallback variant always reports absence.

Iteration helper walks the global domain list invoking a caller supplied callback with opaque data, stopping early and propagating the first nonzero status, otherwise reporting success. The full version holds the list mutex during the walk; the header fallback always reports invalid argument.

Table management offers allocation sized by the domain state count with reference count initialized, release through reference drop with deferred reclamation, and a compute wrapper that derives costs with default flags. Update replaces the domain table pointer and notifies listeners.

Generic netlink entry points provide single domain query by identifier, dump of all domains with resume support, and single table query by domain identifier. Operations are registered for two commands with separate do and dump capabilities and parallel execution allowed.

Single item queries require the identifier attribute; missing attribute or unknown identifier yields invalid argument, allocation failure yields out of memory, and encoding failure yields message too long with the partially built message discarded.

Reply and notification sizing precomputes space from fixed headers plus per CPU entries for domain listings and from identifier plus per state nested entries for tables, scaling linearly with CPU count or state count. Delete notifications reserve only identifier space.

Domain encoding carries identifier, flags, and one entry per member CPU. Table encoding carries domain identifier followed by one nested entry per state with performance, frequency, power, cost and flags values read under read side protection.

Two mutexes separate concerns: one guards the global list membership scanned by lookup and iteration, another serializes table replacement and unregistration against concurrent updates. List walkers assert the update mutex is not held to avoid deadlock ordering.

Performance state arrays are accessed under read side critical sections while updates replace the table pointer with assign semantics and release the old table via reference counting, allowing concurrent readers to see either old or new complete tables.

Dump starts with position zero and resume offset from callback arguments, increments position for each domain, skips those below the offset, and emits one message per remaining domain until buffer exhaustion aborts with truncation status.

Update transitions from validation to locked replacement: acquire update mutex, verify device and domain presence, take a reference on the new table, swap the visible pointer, refresh efficiency markings, drop the old reference, release the mutex, then emit an update notification.

Performance and cost derivation applies only to CPU backed devices; other devices keep zeroed values. Performance scales linearly with frequency relative to maximum capacity. Cost uses a driver callback for artificial domains with strict validity checks, otherwise a scaled power over performance ratio, marking states whose cost does not strictly decrease toward higher frequencies as inefficient.

After table install the updater locates an online CPU in the domain span, obtains its frequency policy, and flags inefficient frequencies there. If any flag is accepted the domain records that inefficiencies should be skipped; missing online CPU or policy access failure only warns and leaves the domain unmarked.

Creation and update notifications multicast the full table encoding while deletion multicasts only the identifier. All three check for event group listeners first and silently discard when none are present or when allocation or header construction fails.

The family exposes two commands with identifier attributes typed as unsigned 32 bit integers and a single multicast group named event. Split operations bind do handlers for both commands and a dump handler for the domain command, with network namespace operation and parallel handling enabled.

Debug hierarchy roots at energy model with one subdirectory per device name. CPU devices add a CPU list file plus flags and identifier files; each state adds a frequency named subdirectory containing frequency, power, cost, performance and inefficiency files, all read only for all users. Alternative build provides no directories.

Attribute append failures during domain or table encoding abort the current message or nested state entry and propagate a truncation status, with dump iteration stopping at the first such failure and single queries freeing the whole message.
When the feature is disabled the header supplies null returning lookup, error returning iteration, and empty notification helpers. Source uses include guards and a fixed log prefix for diagnostics.
Debug initialization creates the top level directory at boot and per device creation populates entries, while removal deletes the device subtree by name lookup.
